title: Colin R. Bundschu
text:
I am a BIDMaP Postdoctoral Fellow in Kristin Persson’s group at UC Berkeley, where I do atomistic calculations of the thermodynamics of disorder in metal oxides for the Materials Project. Before that I did my PhD in applied physics at Cornell, co-advised by Héctor Abruña and Peter Frazier, doing theoretical electrochemistry on metal oxides, and before that I was a software engineer at Microsoft Game Studios, Rockstar Games, and Oculus VR.
My research builds computational tools that converge, in both the mathematical and the numerical sense, so that a chemist can ask for a quantity to a stated tolerance and get it. The program has three parts, described on the Research page:

Exact methods for materials. A library, symat, that represents crystals and molecules as labeled point sets over exact rational arrays, so that symmetry, Voronoi partitions, and coordination are computed exactly and once. Built on it: a from-scratch MACE in numba with analytic Hessians, a geometry relaxer with a symmetry certificate, a bond-valence solver, and a cluster expansion with Wang–Landau sampling.
Electronic structure with a limit. An all-electron, grid-free, parameter-free hierarchy for solids: periodic Hartree–Fock in a generated Gaussian basis, correlated with gap-selected spin-flip EOM-LCCSD, with six explicit convergence knobs and no other setting. Silicon runs on a laptop.
Thermodynamics learned from measurement. Inverting measured disorder thermodynamics to effective cluster interactions with Bayesian inference and conformal-calibrated uncertainty, and choosing the next experiment to shrink that uncertainty.

I was the computational lead on seven experimental collaborations (JACS ×2, Nature Catalysis, PNAS, ACS Catalysis ×2, Chemical Reviews), and I wrote and won two 200,000-GPU-hour NSF ACCESS Maximize allocations and a Schmidt AI for Actionable Matter Modeling grant.

title: Research
text:
The workhorse tools of atomistic calculation run in reasonable amounts of time, but the ones built on density functional theory have theoretically unbounded error and poor convergence in practice. A functional’s error is a property of the functional and cannot be bounded, and the only remedy is another functional, which is a choice, not a limit. Machine-learned potentials make this cheaper, but they inherit the reference they are trained on.
My research takes this on in two ways. First, tools that produce calculations as successive approximations that converge both theoretically and numerically, by using an exact mathematical representation. This is convergence in the sense of constructive analysis: a quantity is known when a procedure brings it within any demanded tolerance. Second, tools that use experimental data to produce surrogate models, so that concrete measurements drive theory rather than the other way around. Underpinning both is a library built on exact symmetry and representation.

title: Research
section: Exact methods for quantum chemistry and materials
text:
Exact methods for quantum chemistry and materials
Why don’t computational chemistry codes converge to better precision, and why don’t you get the same answer when you apply a symmetry operation? I think this is a problem of representation. Rather than carrying atoms as floating-point positions with lattice vectors, symat represents crystals and molecules as labeled point sets over exact rational arrays, so the space group, the Voronoi partition, and the coordination environment are computed exactly and once, with floating point entering only in the consumers. Invalid states are unrepresentable rather than checked, and equivariance is guaranteed by construction.
Built on this representation so far:

A from-scratch numba implementation of MACE with hand-derived forward and backward passes for every block. It reproduces the shipped reference model to 4×10⁻⁷ relative on a 112-atom spinel, which lets relaxation converge to 10⁻⁹ eV and gives Hessians at a cost that makes them routine: phonons, saddle points, and a symmetry certificate that classifies a stationary point by the space group.
A bond-valence solver for oxidation states of molecules and crystals.
A cluster expansion, Wang–Landau Monte Carlo, and a thermodynamics library. On a 112-atom MgAl₂O₄ supercell with the same cutoffs, training set, and held-out set, it agrees with smol and CASM to 10⁻¹² eV and runs canonical Monte Carlo at 1.7–2.7 million steps per second, 4–10× CASM and 40–50× smol’s documented path, on a laptop.

The library is covered by more than 1,700 tests, including finite-difference and equivariance checks on every kernel. Public release is planned for 2027 with a JOSS paper.

title: Research
section: Electronic structure with a limit at an affordable price
text:
Electronic structure with a limit at an affordable price
Can a correlated, all-electron, parameter-free hierarchy for solids be made cheap enough to be general purpose? The approach is periodic Hartree–Fock in a generated even-tempered Gaussian basis (no pseudopotential, no grid, no fitted basis set), an LCCSD/CEPA(0) ground state with amplitudes selected by a gap criterion, and the lowest spin-flip excitation read as the band gap. Low-rank integrals keep memory linear in what is kept, and analytic finite-size tails replace extrapolation fits with lattice sums. Every approximation is a convergence knob with a known limit, and there are six of them: basis degree, number of characters, candidate pool, kept amplitudes, ladder order, and rank floor. No other setting exists.
On silicon, produced on one laptop under one frozen protocol: the all-electron Hartree–Fock reference gives Γ→X 6.77 eV and Γ→Γ 9.27 eV, triplet CIS with the analytic tail gives 2.39 and 4.82 eV, and the correlated spin-flip read gives 1.12 and 3.79 eV against measured values of 1.17 and 3.4 eV. Each step down the hierarchy moves the right way, by the right order of magnitude, with no parameter touched. The aim is not better accuracy on silicon but the existence of a limit.

title: Research
text:
Thermodynamics on labeled data
Can the thermodynamics of disorder in oxides be learned from measurements directly, with the model’s error estimated from held-out data and the next experiment chosen to shrink it? The cluster expansion is linear in its interactions, and the correlation vector of a configuration is its sufficient statistic, so configurations sampled under one set of interactions reweight exactly to any other. One sampling pass per system therefore serves a whole Bayesian posterior over the interactions, with uncertainty calibrated by conformal statistics. Site occupancies versus temperature, mixing enthalpies, and transition temperatures are three projections of the same interactions, and each measurement can be chosen in advance to reduce the model’s uncertainty the most.
The first systems are non-magnetic double perovskites (La₂HfMgO₆, La₂ZnTiO₆, La₂MgZrO₆, Ba₂ZrSnO₆), whose B-site disorder fraction versus temperature I predicted from the cluster expansion and which A-Lab at LBNL has synthesized and is annealing to measure.

title: Software
text:
symat
Exact representations for atomistic computation. Crystals and molecules are labeled point sets over exact rational arrays, and every consumer is built on that one representation: a space-group symmetry library, Voronoi and coordination analysis, a bond-valence solver, a cluster expansion with Wang–Landau Monte Carlo, a ground-up numba implementation of MACE with analytic gradients and Hessians, and a second-order geometry relaxer with a symmetry certificate. Python and numba, with CUDA kernels via cuBLAS. More than 1,700 tests, including finite-difference and equivariance checks on every kernel.
Private repository pending publication. Public release planned for 2027 with a JOSS paper. Code walkthrough available on request.

title: Software
text:
Electronic-structure solver
A parameter-free, grid-free, all-electron electronic-structure hierarchy for solids: periodic Hartree–Fock in a generated Gaussian basis, correlated with gap-selected spin-flip EOM-LCCSD, with Cholesky low-rank integrals and analytic finite-size tails. Six convergence knobs with known limits and no other setting. Silicon runs on a laptop. See Research for the current numbers.
Unreleased. A preprint and the code are in preparation.

title: Software
text:
mass-gap
github.com/ColinBundschu/mass-gap. Constructive lattice gauge theory in Lean 4: about 490,000 lines with no external packages and no sorry, axiom, opaque, unsafe, noncomputable, or native_decide in source. Proves finite-truncation spectral gaps, SU(N) representation theory, and the weak-coupling chain. The uniform-in-volume gap and the continuum limit are stated as open.

title: Software
text:
Spinel ORR dataset and pipeline
An 80,000-calculation solvated-DFT pipeline across 442 spinel compositions, run on ALCF, NREL, DeltaAI, and Jetstream2, with neural surrogates for intermediate energies and an ML-guided scheme that chooses which expensive calculations to run. The dataset of 80,000 solvated joint-DFT free energies is public on Materials Cloud (DOI 10.24435/materialscloud:ka-8a).

title: About
text:
I came to science as an outsider from industry. I studied computer science at Harvey Mudd College, then spent four years as a software engineer and game designer at Microsoft Game Studios (Crackdown 3, Ryse), Rockstar Games (multiplayer systems for Red Dead Redemption 2), and Oculus VR (project lead for Oculus Arcade and the first Rift retail demo). The pragmatic habits of that work, shipping tested code on a schedule and treating “so what?” as a legitimate question, are the habits I brought to research.
I did my M.S. and Ph.D. in Applied and Engineering Physics at Cornell, co-advised by Héctor Abruña and Peter Frazier, doing theoretical electrochemistry and ML-guided computation on metal oxides, supported by an NDSEG Fellowship. I was the computational lead on seven experimental collaborations spanning oxygen reduction, CO₂ reduction, hydrogen oxidation, and fuel-cell degradation. My thesis predicted an alkaline oxygen-reduction pathway on spinel oxides whose computed onset potential matched experiment where the standard pathway missed by 0.7 V.
Since July 2025 I have been a BIDMaP Postdoctoral Fellow in Kristin Persson’s group at UC Berkeley, working on the Materials Project and on the thermodynamics of disorder in metal oxides. I have written and won two 200,000-GPU-hour NSF ACCESS Maximize allocations and a Schmidt AI for Actionable Matter Modeling grant.
Reading Errett Bishop’s constructive analysis is the reason my work is first-principles and parameter-free: a quantity is known when a procedure brings it within any demanded tolerance, and I think computational chemistry should be held to that standard.
I was born and raised in Denver.
